appraisal_events.evidence: vieillir en quelques mois, s'absorber dans un chagrin... il se voyait avec sa fille dans le dernier bas-fond, et ses manières en avaient reçu... cette humilité, ce respect pour ceux qui se trouvaient au-dessus de lui
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator directly depicts M. Vinteuil's grief-stricken decline and his internalized social self-abasement, in which he comes to place himself and his daughter at the very bottom of local esteem because of the rumors about her.

appraisal_events.evidence: Quel homme exquis... avec la même enthousiaste vénération qui tient de spirituelles et jolies bourgeoises en respect et sous le charme d'une duchesse, fût-elle laide et sotte. Quel homme exquis ! Quel malheur qu'il ait fait un mariage tout à fait déplacé.
appraisal_events.explanation: Vinteuil enthusiastically admires Swann's personal charm while in the same breath condemning his marriage as socially unsuitable; the narrator frames the admiration itself as a somewhat indiscriminate, snobbish reflex, and notes that the narrator's parents echo the same judgment hypocritically.

status_effects.explanation: Vinteuil comes to see himself and his daughter as occupying the lowest social rank and adopts a newly humble, deferential manner toward those he once considered his equals or inferiors.
His grief over his wife's death, compounded by the scandal surrounding his daughter, is described as leaving him visibly dying of sorrow.
Swann is praised as 'exquis,' though the admiration is narrated with an ironic edge that keeps the elevation modest.
Swann's marriage is judged 'tout à fait déplacé' by Vinteuil and echoed by the narrator's parents, marking a local social discredit alongside the personal admiration.

ambiguities: Vinteuil's admiration of Swann is narrated with an ironic comparison to bourgeoises dazzled by a duchess regardless of merit, leaving it unclear whether the narrator fully endorses the admiration or is gently exposing its snobbish, indiscriminate quality.
